introduction-when-b-trees-fail.core: A B-tree needs a single sort order. Containers (JSON, arrays, text) and shapes (geometry, ranges) have none, so Postgres offers GIN, GiST, BRIN and Hash indexes, each matched to a different question.

first_principles.problem: A B-tree answers "equal to" and "between" on values that line up on one axis. It can't answer "which documents contain color=blue", "which shops are within 2 miles" or "which posts have tag X", because there's no meaningful "greater than" for coordinates or containers.
truths: B-trees depend on a total, one-dimensional ordering.
Containment, overlap and proximity aren't orderings.
An index must mirror the question it answers.
derivation: For "contains element" (JSONB, arrays, full text) use an **inverted index**: **GIN**.
For shapes, ranges and nearest-neighbour use **bounding-box trees**: **GiST**.
For huge, naturally ordered append-only tables use **block summaries**: **BRIN**.
For exact equality only, **Hash**.
Also consider structural tricks for any type: **covering** and **partial** indexes, and remember **over-indexing** costs.

analogy.title: Different ways to find things in a city
analogy.story: A street-number index (B-tree) works for "house 42 on Main Street". To find "every shop selling coffee" you need a directory by product (GIN). To find "everything within 2 km" you need a map divided into districts (GiST).
analogy.breaks: City directories rarely change. Database indexes are updated on every write, so each type also has a write cost.

points: B-trees need a single sort order.

check.q: Why can't a B-tree index geographic proximity?
check.a: Proximity in 2-D has no single linear order. 'North' isn't greater than 'West', so a sorted tree can't group nearby points.

gin-indexes-the-inverted-index.core: GIN breaks each container value (array, JSONB, tsvector) into elements and maps every element to the rows containing it, so containment queries are set lookups and intersections instead of scans. It's fast to read and costly to write.

first_principles.problem: `WHERE tags @> ARRAY['sql','database']` must otherwise open every row and parse every array. On millions of rows that's seconds per query.
truths: A container holds many searchable elements.
Queries ask which rows contain certain elements.
Updating many index entries per row is expensive.
derivation: **Invert** the data: element → list of rows.
Answer `@>` (contains all) by **intersecting** lists, and `&&` (overlaps) by **union**.
Pay on writes: each changed container updates many entries.
Buffer writes in a **pending list** (`gin_pending_list_limit`, default 4 MB), merged in bulk on vacuum or when full.

analogy.title: A book's back-of-book index
analogy.story: Instead of reading every page to find "volcano", you look up "volcano" in the index and get pages 12, 87 and 203. To find pages mentioning both "volcano" and "lava", you intersect two short lists.
mapping: Reprinting the index for a new edition
analogy.breaks: A book index is built once. GIN must update on every insert, which is why it buffers changes and why heavy writers see merge spikes.

check.a: A GIN index on the column and queries using @>. Watch write overhead and gin_pending_list_limit on busy tables.

gist-indexes-the-shape-of-data.core: GiST groups nearby or overlapping objects into nested bounding boxes, so a spatial or range query can skip whole regions that can't match. It powers PostGIS, range overlaps and nearest-neighbour search.

first_principles.problem: "All coffee shops within 2 miles" or "bookings that overlap this date range" can't use sort order. Without a structure that understands space, the database computes distance or overlap for every row.
truths: Nearby objects can be enclosed by one bounding rectangle.
If a rectangle doesn't touch your search area, nothing inside it can match.
derivation: Wrap nearby items in **minimum bounding rectangles**, and wrap those in bigger rectangles: a tree (R-tree via the GiST framework).
Search from the top: **prune** any box that doesn't overlap the query area.
Descend only into overlapping boxes and **recheck** leaves (possible false positives).
Use `<->` with `ORDER BY … LIMIT` for **K-nearest-neighbour** without computing every distance.
Prefer GiST for **write-heavy** full-text and spatial data, and GIN for read-heavy containment.

analogy.title: Organising a map collection
analogy.story: You can't sort maps alphabetically by "where". So you put European maps in one cabinet, Asian in another, then group by country inside. To find maps covering Lyon, you skip the Asia cabinet entirely.
analogy.breaks: Cabinets don't overlap. Bounding boxes can, so a query may need to descend into several branches, and that's why GiST reads can be slightly slower than GIN.

check.q: Why can GiST return false positives?
check.a: Bounding boxes approximate shapes, so a box can overlap the query area while the actual object inside doesn't. Leaves are rechecked.

covering-indexes-the-shortcut.core: A covering index stores the columns a query needs inside the index (INCLUDE), so the database answers from the index alone (index-only scan) without jumping to the table. It only works fully when VACUUM keeps the visibility map current.

first_principles.problem: A normal index lookup is two steps: find the key in the index, then jump to the table (heap) for the other columns. For thousands of matching rows scattered across pages, those jumps are thousands of random reads.
truths: If the needed data is already in the index, the heap is unnecessary.
Postgres must still know each row version is visible.
derivation: Add the selected columns as **INCLUDE** payload in the index leaves.
The query is satisfied from the index: **index-only scan**, often 10–100× faster.
Prefer `INCLUDE` over adding to the key: payload isn't sorted, so inner nodes stay small.
Keep the **visibility map** current with VACUUM, or Postgres falls back to heap checks.

analogy.title: A contact card with the phone number on it
analogy.story: A name index that only says "see filing cabinet B, folder 512" forces a walk to the cabinet. If the index card already shows the phone number, you're done without leaving your desk.
mapping: Index card pointing to a folder
analogy.breaks: An index card is always current. In Postgres the index can't tell if a row version is visible, so it relies on the visibility map, which only VACUUM updates.

example.title: Heap Fetches that won't go away
example.scenario: A covering index was added, but EXPLAIN still shows thousands of heap fetches.

steps.label: Puzzle
steps.detail: Pages aren't marked all-visible because vacuum hasn't run since recent updates.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: `VACUUM ANALYZE users` turns it into a true index-only scan.

example.outcome: the query never touches the table and runs many times faster.

check.q: Why use INCLUDE instead of adding columns to the index key?
check.a: INCLUDE columns live only in leaves and aren't sorted, which keeps the tree smaller. Key columns are needed only if you filter or sort by them.

partial-indexes-the-specialist.core: A partial index only indexes rows matching a WHERE condition, typically the small hot subset you actually query. It's tiny, fits in RAM and is cheap to maintain, but queries must include a matching condition to use it.

first_principles.problem: An orders table has 1 billion rows, but only 10 million are active and queried constantly. A full index covers all billion: gigabytes in RAM, slower writes, long rebuilds, mostly for rows nobody looks at.
truths: Most queries hit a small, well-defined subset.
Index size drives RAM use and write cost.
The planner only uses an index it can prove is relevant.
derivation: Add a **WHERE** to the index: `… WHERE status = 'active'`, which makes it about 100× smaller.
Write cost falls: only rows in the subset touch it.
The query's WHERE must **imply** the index's predicate. Verify with `EXPLAIN`.
Use it for **queues** (`processed = false`), **soft deletes** (`deleted_at IS NULL`), and **unique among active rows**.

analogy.title: A VIP guest list
analogy.story: Instead of a phone book of everyone in the city, the doorman keeps a short list of tonight's VIPs. It's quick to check and easy to update, but useless for someone who isn't on tonight's list.
analogy.breaks: A doorman can improvise. The planner can't: if it can't prove your query implies the predicate, it won't use the index.

check.q: Why might a partial index be ignored for WHERE order_id = $1?
check.a: Nothing in the query proves status = 'active', so the planner can't safely use an index that excludes other statuses.

the-cost-of-over-indexing.core: Every index is paid for on every write, takes buffer-pool memory and gives the planner more chances to choose badly. Audit unused indexes (idx_scan = 0) and drop them carefully.

first_principles.problem: "More indexes = faster queries" is a common junior instinct. A table with 10 indexes turns each INSERT into 11 writes, crowds hot data out of RAM, and can slow the very reads the indexes were meant to help.
truths: Each index must be updated when its columns change.
Buffer pool memory is finite and shared.
The planner chooses among indexes using statistics.
derivation: Count **write amplification**: 1 row write + N index writes, plus more lock contention.
Count **space**: unused indexes evict hot pages from `shared_buffers`, causing misses.
Watch **planner confusion**: overlapping indexes and stale stats lead to bad choices.
**Audit**: `pg_stat_user_indexes` where `idx_scan = 0`, excluding PK/unique constraints, sorted by size.
Drop in a quiet window, watch `pg_stat_statements` for regressions, and remember stats reset on restart.

analogy.title: Too many filing systems
analogy.story: An office that files every document in ten different cabinets (by date, author, client, colour…) spends most of its time filing. The cabinets fill the room so there's no space for what's actually used, and staff waste time deciding which cabinet to search.
analogy.breaks: Unused cabinets are visible. Unused indexes are invisible unless you query the statistics views.

example.title: A quarterly index audit
example.scenario: An events table with 14 indexes and slowing ingestion.

steps.label: Find
